Kindly
kīnd'lĭ
adv. (with kindness; benevolently; also adj., natural, according to kind)
Old English gecyndelic, natural, according to one's kind — the older sense survives in kindly fruits of the earth. The moral sense follows: to act kindly is to act as one of the same kind.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version has a habit with this word that is easy to miss and hard to unlearn once seen: it almost never lets kindly stand alone. Abraham's servant asks Laban and Bethuel, “if ye will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me” (Gen 24:49). Jacob asks the same of Joseph, deal kindly and truly with me. The spies swear it to Rahab, we will deal kindly and truly with thee. The pairing is not decoration; it is the Hebrew chesed we-emeth, covenant-love and faithfulness, the two together, and the second word is what keeps the first from being sentiment. Naomi blesses her daughters in law with it: “The LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me” (Rut 1:8). In the New Testament Paul makes it a family word: “Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another” (Rom 12:10) — where the Greek compounds the word for family affection, so that the church is to feel toward one another what kinsmen feel, and then to go past it in giving honour away.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines kindly as with good will; with a disposition to make others happy or to oblige; benevolently; and in the older sense, according to nature or kind.

KINDLY, adv. With good will; with a disposition to make others happy, or to oblige; benevolently; favorably.

KINDLY, a. Homogeneal; congenial; of the same nature.

2. Mild; bland; softening; as kindly showers.

Key Scripture

Gen 24:49 — "And now if ye will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me: and if not, tell me; that I may turn to the right hand, or to the left."

Rut 1:8 — "And Naomi said unto her two daughters in law, Go, return each to her mother's house: the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me."

Rom 12:10 — "Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;"

Modern Corruption

Kindness severed from truth becomes mere agreeableness, and the Authorized Version's persistent pairing — kindly and truly — is the standing correction to it.

expand to see more

Four times in the narrative books the phrase runs the same way: deal kindly and truly. The Hebrew behind it, chesed we-emeth, is the pair that Exodus 34 puts in God's own self-description — abundant in goodness and truth — and that John 1:14 carries into Greek when the Word is full of grace and truth. The two are given together because either one alone deforms. Truth without kindness is the accuracy of an enemy. Kindness without truth is what a man offers when he has decided that the other party cannot bear reality, and it is therefore a quiet form of contempt. The therapeutic register of the present hour makes the second error systematically: to be kind is redefined as to affirm, and to withhold agreement is redefined as a species of harm, with the result that the only remaining way to love a man is to tell him nothing he does not already believe. Scripture's categories are firmer and gentler at once. Faithful are the wounds of a friend, says Proverbs, and the deceitful kisses of an enemy are set opposite them. A church that has learned to say kindly and truly as one phrase will not have to choose between being loving and being honest, because it will have stopped believing the two can be separated.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chesed (H2617), covenant mercy, steadfast love, constantly paired with emeth (H571), truth; Greek philostorgos (G5387), tenderly loving as kin.

expand to see more

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant kindness, loyal love; the great Old Testament word for God's bond-keeping mercy, rendered lovingkindness in the Psalms; Ruth 1:8.

Hebrew emeth (H571) — firmness, truth, faithfulness; joined to chesed in the formula deal kindly and truly; Genesis 24:49.

Greek philostorgos (G5387) — loving with the natural affection of family; Paul's one use of it makes the church a household; Romans 12:10.

Usage

"“Deal kindly and truly with my master” — the pairing that keeps kindness from becoming sentiment."

"“The LORD deal kindly with you” — Naomi's blessing on Orpah and Ruth."

"“Be kindly affectioned one to another” — family affection made a church duty."
